name: v0
subcategory: AI coding agents and developer workspaces
tagline: Generate React components from a brief and write them into a local project with previews

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: $5 model/usage credits per month plus 7 messages per day.

tiers.name: Plus
tiers.limits: $30 monthly credits/user plus a $2 daily credit grant on days the user logs in.

tiers.name: Business
tiers.limits: $30 monthly credits/user plus a $2 daily credit grant on login; business controls.

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Custom seats, credits, controls and support.

pricing.billingTerms: monthly only; no public annual plan
pricing.hiddenCosts: Usage is metered by model and cache type. Published rates range from $0.20/M input and $1.20/M output for Mini to $10/M input and $50/M output for Max Fast; teams can buy shared extra credits.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For v0, generate React components from a brief and write them into a local project with previews. The hard boundary is vercel models, design tuning, component data, deployment, and ecosystem integration, plus frontier models, context infrastructure, and execution safety.
coreLoopDIY: Generate React components from a brief, write them into a local project with previews, index the repository, propose reviewable patches, run approved commands, and preserve an auditable session log.
whatYouLose: Vercel models, design tuning, component data, deployment, and ecosystem integration
moatNotes: frontier models, context infrastructure, and execution safety
ongoingBurden: model changes, indexing, prompt injection, tool permissions, sandboxing, evaluation, telemetry choices, and IDE compatibility
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for v0 because the UI can be copied, but high-quality code models, context ranking, safe execution, and constant evaluation are the product. The recurring cost buys model changes, indexing, prompt injection, tool permissions, sandboxing, evaluation, telemetry choices, and IDE compatibility, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Continue
priorArt.desc: Active open-source coding-assistant framework for IDEs and multiple model providers.

alternatives.name: Dyad
alternatives.desc: Prompt a React app, preview it locally, then own the files and the bugs.

facts.engines: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, OpenRouter-compatible providers and local Ollama
facts.dataFormat: Generated project source and app metadata stay on the computer; prompts and selected context go to the chosen provider unless a local model is used
facts.gapVsPaid: It is a broader local app generator, but it is less polished for component-specific generation, design-system reuse and Vercel-native handoff than v0.
facts.setupBlocker: A model-provider API key or a separately installed and configured local Ollama model

alternatives.name: OpenUI
alternatives.desc: Describe a component and see it rendered live, with output as HTML, React, or Svelte.

facts.install: Docker image or Python and uv source installation
facts.engines: OpenAI, Groq, LiteLLM-compatible providers, LocalAI and Ollama
facts.dataFormat: Generated code and session state live in the running instance and browser; prompts go to the selected model backend
facts.gapVsPaid: It lacks v0's polished component library workflow, project persistence and direct Vercel deployment path.
facts.setupBlocker: Docker or a Python environment plus an API key, unless a compatible local model server is already running

alternatives.name: Onlook
alternatives.desc: Visual AI editor for React apps: click an element, restyle it, let the model write the code.

facts.install: Hosted signup, or self-host with Bun or Docker plus Supabase configuration
facts.engines: OpenRouter plus configurable code-edit services such as Morph or Relace
facts.dataFormat: Project code lives in the workspace or sandbox; application metadata and assets use the configured Supabase instance
facts.gapVsPaid: It works best around a real React or Next.js codebase and is weaker than v0 at turning a brief directly into a polished standalone component.
facts.setupBlocker: Hosted access may be gated; self-hosting needs Bun or Docker, Supabase and several environment variables

rejectedAlternatives.name: bolt.diy
rejectedAlternatives.desc: MIT source, but its WebContainers runtime needs a commercial licence for production business use.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Continue
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Acquired and read-only, and an editor agent is not a component generator with live previews.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Premium plan and a single-repository coding assistant DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for v0 in an empty repository.
Use TypeScript, Node.js 22, a VS Code extension, SQLite, and one user-supplied model API; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: generate React components from a brief, write them into a local project with previews, index the repository, propose reviewable patches, run approved commands, and preserve an auditable session log.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create a VS Code sidebar with chat, selected-code actions, repository search, and a patch preview.
Index only the open repository and respect .gitignore plus a separate assistant ignore file.
Require explicit approval before reading outside the workspace or running any command.
Represent edits as unified diffs with accept, reject, partial apply, undo, and Git status checks.
Capture tool calls, model requests, command output, and patch decisions in a local session log.
Add token and cost estimates, provider errors, cancellation, tests, and an offline data-flow diagram.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out training or reproducing a frontier coding model.
Deliberately leave out unattended command execution outside a sandbox.
Deliberately leave out cloud workspaces, team policy, and enterprise support.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
